items.note: Three mukhamaṇḍapas on east, north and south lead to the gūḍhamaṇḍapa; a flight of steps precedes the east one.
Mukhamaṇḍapa mouldings: rājasemaka fillet, vedikā balustrade with ghaṭapallava stambhikās and apsarās, chajjikā, mañcikā and ghaṇṭikā.
Celestial maidens are slim yet ample, tall and graceful, standing on stylised lotuses in abhaṅga stances.
Unusual female figure with a staff and a camel on the vedikā of the east mukhamaṇḍapa.
Figure read as Nirṛti, wife of Virūpākṣa; the reins signifying pāśa are important in the context of Śaiva Siddhānta.
Doorways of the mukhamaṇḍapas: śākhā types, river goddesses and dikpālas as door guardians on the peḍya; Cāmuṇḍā and Gaṇeśa on the south door jambs.
South mukhamaṇḍapa lintel with foliage scrolls, mālādhāras and lalāṭabimbas of Gaṇeśa and Lakṣmī.
Mātṛkā panel above the south door shows nine goddesses; Brahmāṇi and Māheśvarī described.
Above the mātṛkās are male gods in five projecting niches and the navagrahas in four recessed niches.
Nine planets in personified forms, paired in niches; Rāhu, Ketu and Śani grouped as malefic planets.
Gūḍhamaṇḍapa has three entrance doors; main entrance from the east mukhamaṇḍapa; vestibule with niches and sculpted pillars.
Four main pillars are square, then polygonal and circular, classed as miśraka.
Vidyādhara figures with swords and shields follow the Samrāṅgaṇasūtradhāra description; early parallel at Ajanta Cave 17.
Samrāṅgaṇasūtradhāra on the hierarchy of yakṣas, gandharvas, nāgas and vidyādharas; the artisan seems well-versed in canonical injunctions.
Pillar niches show Śiva and Tapasvinī Pārvatī with jaṭāmukuṭa.
Pārvatī in the pillar niches with four hands, Śivaliṅga and Gaṇeśa; Aparājitapṛcchā cited.
A stone feature in the gūḍhamaṇḍapa may have kept the drum; the time-keeper was an important person in the temple retinue who struck the drum at regular intervals.
Gūḍhamaṇḍapa ceiling of the nābhichanda class, concentric circles in an octagonal frame with kīrtimukhas.
Brass cover of the Śivaliṅga fashioned as a mukhaliṅga, presented by Khanderao Appaji, a general of Mahadji Scindia.

items.note: The vedī in front of the temple is a flat-roofed square building ventilated by stone grills on all sides.
Cunningham thought the vedī was used for preaching the Vedas; gives its dimensions (23 feet square inside, four pillars).
refs: Cunningham, Report of Tours in Bundelkhand and Malwa 1874-75 and 1876-77, p. 69

items.note: Cunningham: massive trellises, ceiling by overlapping stones, building still in excellent preservation after eight centuries.
refs: Cunningham, Report of Tours in Bundelkhand and Malwa 1874-75 and 1876-77, p. 69

items.note: By tradition the king ordered the vedī built after the temple for a yajña; its ventilation and seating suggest ritual use, perhaps with music and dance.
Quoted report: temple in a spacious square courtyard with a dwarf compound wall decorated with carvings and seats with backrests.
Quoted report: four entrances, principal one east, each with steps and doorkeeper; of eight attendant shrines only six standing.
Quoted report: Muhammad Tughluq between AD 1336-38 damaged the attendant temples and erected a mosque at the back; Persian inscriptions record it.
Western rear converted into a mosque in the 14th century; two archways served as symbolic entrances; one houses a Garuḍāsana Viṣṇu image.
Beglar 1871-72: temple on a paved raised platform; seven minor temples once stood around, now gone or converted into dwellings.
refs: Beglar, Report of a Tour in Bundelkhand and Malwa 1871-72, pp. 84-86

items.note: Beglar describes the masjid at the back: hall with flat roof on four rows of Hindu pillars, mihrab niche, masons' marks proving the pillars Hindu.
refs: Beglar, Report of a Tour in Bundelkhand and Malwa 1871-72, pp. 84-86

items.note: Beglar records the legend that Aurangzeb ordered demolition and a masjid; Mahadeva appeared in a dream; temple spared and masjid built at the back; temple frequented by both Hindus and Muhammadans.

claim.value: Aurangzeb ordered demolition, was deterred by Mahadeva in a dream, a masjid was built at the back

refs: Beglar, Report of a Tour in Bundelkhand and Malwa 1871-72, pp. 84-86

items.note: Pande says Beglar erred: the masjid was built by Muhammad Tughlak in the 14th century and the inscriptions record his name.
Cunningham: the temple is built of hard fine-grained red sandstone quarried in the hill close by.
refs: Cunningham, Report of Tours in Bundelkhand and Malwa 1874-75 and 1876-77, p. 68

items.note: Cunningham: north-west corner temple and western bedi knocked down in Muhammad Tughlak's time; masjid recorded by inscriptions dated 737 and 739 Hijira; west gateway built of old materials.
refs: Cunningham, Report of Tours in Bundelkhand and Malwa 1874-75 and 1876-77, p. 68

items.note: Local tradition: in 1325 CE after the conquest of Udayapur Sultan Muhammad Tughluq ordered the temple razed; only part of the Vedic hall on the west became a mosque.

claim.value: Tughluq ordered razing in 1325 CE; temple not razed, part of the Vedic hall made a mosque

items.note: Ghariyālon Kā Makān: house of the temple time-keepers who struck the gong to keep time for the rituals.
Living temple with morning and evening pūja and aarti, special pūjas on request, fairs on Śaiva festivals, main festival Śivarātri and Sāvan Mondays.
Pisanhārī kā Mandir, a later plain temple said to have been built by a flour-grinder who saved money; shows both royal and humble patronage.
Seated Umā-Maheśvara image inside the Pisanhārī kā Mandir, coated with soot, with Umā on Śiva's lap and mounts below.
Endnote cites Bühler's 'Udepur Prasasti of the Kings of Malva' in Epigraphia Indica vol. 1 (ed. Burgess, ASI 1983), p. 238.
refs: G. Buhler, Udepur Prasasti of the Kings of Malva, Epigraphia Indica vol. 1, p. 238

items.note: Temple as a three-dimensional model of the cosmic body of god (vāstupuruṣa); understanding it requires the philosophy of the Āgamaśāstras as well as the Śilpaśāstras.
Śaiva cult background: Paśupati cult in the epics, foreign rulers drawn to Śaivism, Śaivism a major Gupta-period cult.
Four Śaiva schools named; Śaiva Siddhāntis dominated Central India and the South; Bhoja Paramāra wrote the Tattvaprakāśa on Śaiva Siddhānta in the 11th century CE.
Pāśupatas, perhaps the most ancient Śaiva cult, are dualistic: pati, paśu and pāśa.
Thirty-six tattvas of Kashmir Śaivism, beyond Sāṃkhya's twenty-five: Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Sadvidyā and the kañcukas.
The first five tattvas constitute the pure order, the śuddha addhvā.
